planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall into gravelly, seasonally moist clay or volcanic soil that dries by summer, replicating vernal-pool-margin and foothill-grassland conditions.

directions: A foothill and valley-grassland bulb carrying branched spikes of cream-white, bell-shaped flowers each marked with a greenish gland spot, this death camas fills a seasonally-moist-to-dry niche distinct from garden bulbs that need summer water. Every part of the plant is toxic if eaten, so site it away from livestock pasture and away from areas where bulbs could be mistaken for wild onion. It wants wet feet through winter and spring bloom, then a dry summer dormancy with no supplemental irrigation.

planting.note: Divide rhizomes in early spring into consistently moist, mineral-rich soil over serpentine or ultramafic bedrock in dappled shade along a seep or streamside.

directions: A Klamath-Siskiyou endemic false hellebore restricted to serpentine and ultramafic seeps, this species carries narrow, less-pleated leaves than the widespread Veratrum californicum and tolerates the unusual low-calcium, heavy-metal mineral chemistry of serpentine soil. All plant parts are highly toxic if ingested, so keep it away from grazing animals and curious pets. It needs a constantly moist, seep-fed site and will decline if the soil dries out even briefly during the growing season.

subcategory: coastal bluff and dune swale perennial

planting.note: Divide rhizomes in early spring into moist, sandy, humus-rich soil in a coastal-fog-belt site with mild, cool summers; inland heat and dry air cause scorch.

directions: A narrow northern California coastal endemic found in moist swales and seeps behind foggy coastal dunes and bluffs, this false hellebore bears the genus's tallest flower spikes topped with distinctively fringed, greenish-white petals. It is adapted to cool, fog-moderated summers and struggles with inland heat, so it suits only true coastal-climate gardens. As with all Veratrum, every part is toxic if ingested, so keep it out of reach of children, pets, and livestock.

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall into consistently moist, mineral, serpentine-influenced soil at a seep or bog margin that stays wet through the growing season.

directions: A Klamath-Siskiyou bulb from serpentine bogs and seeps, this rush lily sends up a tall wand of small white, lily-like flowers in mid to late summer when most other bulbs in the genus have finished. Unlike the dry-summer bulbs more common in western gardens, it needs its roots kept wet through the whole growing season, making it a good fit for a bog garden or constantly moist seep bed rather than a typical xeric bulb border. It is uncommon in cultivation, so source nursery-propagated bulbs rather than wild material.

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall into consistently moist, mineral, serpentine-influenced seep or bog soil; wants more open sun than H. alba.

directions: A rare Klamath-Siskiyou serpentine-seep endemic, this rush lily carries notably larger, showier white flowers than its relative H. alba on a comparably tall summer-blooming spike. It is restricted in the wild to a handful of serpentine wetland sites and is a genuine rarity in cultivation, best treated as a specialist bog-garden subject for collectors with a wet, mineral-soil seep rather than a general-purpose border plant. Keep soil saturated through summer; it will not tolerate a dry-down like typical western bulbs.

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall into lean, well-drained foothill clay or loam that dries completely in summer; give full sun and no summer irrigation.

directions: A grassland and foothill soap plant with notably narrower, more upright leaves than the widespread Chlorogalum pomeridianum, this species opens small white, star-shaped flowers in the evening in summer, pollinated mainly by moths. Like its relatives it stores up a fibrous-coated bulb traditionally used for soap and cordage by California Indigenous peoples, and it needs the same dry summer dormancy to thrive — wet summer soil rots the bulb. Pair it with other summer-dry California grassland bulbs rather than irrigated border perennials.

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall into lean, rocky, serpentine-influenced foothill soil with sharp drainage and full sun; give no summer water once dormant.

directions: Restricted to the serpentine-derived Red Hills soils of the Sierra Nevada foothills, this soap plant carries the largest, showiest flowers in the genus, opening white with a purple midstripe in the evening and closing by morning. It shares the dry-summer bulb dormancy of its relatives but additionally needs the low-fertility, heavy-metal mineral chemistry typical of serpentine substrate, making ordinary garden loam a poor stand-in. It is uncommon in commerce; source from a specialty California native-bulb grower.

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall into lean, rocky, caliche or limestone-derived soil with sharp drainage and full sun, mimicking Edwards Plateau and Chihuahuan Desert scrub.

directions: A little-grown Texas and Chihuahuan Desert bulb related to the historically important sabadilla-seed insecticide plant, this species sends up a slender spike of small greenish flowers from narrow, grass-like basal leaves over rocky limestone scrub. All plant parts contain toxic alkaloids, so handle bulbs with care and site it away from edible plantings and curious pets. It needs sharp caliche or limestone drainage and essentially no summer water once established, fitting a xeric Edwards Plateau or Chihuahuan native bed.
